 Rising federal loan bills under new Trump rules put financial squeeze on California students 
 by 
 William Melhado • EdSource 
 Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 a.m. Nov. 16, 2026, 1:21 p.m.

 President Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order alongside Secretary of Education Linda McMahon in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Thursday, March 20, 2025. (Photo by Ben Curtis/Associated Press) 
 This article first appeared in EdSource. 
 When Vincent Rasso saw how much his monthly student loan payments would climb to repay the nearly $30,000 he borrowed, the UC Riverside graduate decided he couldn’t afford to travel to visit his family for Thanksgiving. 
 “How do you plan for another $400 payment that is going to be put on you every month?” Rasso, director of government relations for the University of California Student Association, said. “It’s made me question, in the short term, what sort of things I should be cutting back on.”
 Rising inflation and housing costs, paired with sweeping changes to federal student loan policies, are putting California students in a financial bind. Monthly loan bills are rising for many borrowers, while others are rethinking whether they can afford graduate or doctoral programs.
 President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated the Grad PLUS program, which allowed graduate students to borrow up to the cost of tuition, and lowered loan limits for graduate and professional students. It also established two new repayment plans. For Rasso, both options will at least double his $160 monthly payments.
 The impact of the policy changes, which took effect this summer, have been far-reaching, advocates say, and have fostered distrust in the federal government among students over a confusing rollout. Experts say new limits on federal loan amounts will push more borrowers to seek out more expensive and riskier loans from private lenders. 
 “These changes will restrict access to these pathways, which is both unfair and harmful to society,” said Sara Partridge, associate director of higher education policy at the Center for American Progress (CAP), a left-leaning think tank.
 CAP’s analysis found that Black borrowers are estimated to pay 98% more when they switch from the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) Plan to the Repayment Assistance Plan, one of the two new repayment plans. 
 The Trump administration argued that the changes will make higher education more affordable by discouraging excessive borrowing and pressuring universities to lower tuition. The Trump administration estimated total taxpayer savings of more than $409 billion, in part, by eliminating loan forgiveness programs. 
 A Department of Education spokesperson cited an American Enterprise Institute report   identifying more than 50 graduate schools that have reduced tuition since the law passed. However, some reductions apply only to select students, such as alumni or university employees’ family members.
 ‘The alarm bells are ringing’
 One in five borrowers, who hold some of the total $1.9 trillion in student loan debt, are in default.  
 But the federal changes meant to address the massive debt have created chaos and confusion for borrowers, said Natalia Abrams, the founder of the nonprofit Student Debt Crisis Center. 
 “Years ago, borrowers signed up to what they thought was a 20-year program, only to have it taken away from them and be forced with options that are far more expensive,” Abrams said, referring to the SAVE Plan. “Borrowers have received so much conflicting information.” 
 Student borrower advocates have warned that the changes could ultimately increase costs to repay loans. Aissa Canchola Bañez, the policy director at the advocacy group Protect Borrowers, said the cuts made to the student loan system were the third largest in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which also made significant cuts to Medicaid and food assistance programs.

 “The alarm bells are ringing so much harder, faster, louder within this group of borrowers,” Canchola Bañez said. “They are actively thinking through how to cover what used to be a $50 monthly bill, when it is now multiple hundreds of dollars.”
 California borrowers face one of the highest payment jumps in the U.S. 
 Compared to other Americans, borrowers in California will face one of the largest jumps in student loan payments — nearly $3,000 annually — when they switch to the new Repayment Assistance Plan, according to CAP’s estimates. 
 The University of California says it opposes the loan changes because the policies will make it more difficult to obtain federal loans, which will impact lower-income UC students.
 “At a time when our state and country face affordability challenges and workforce shortages, limiting access to student loans and other financial aid risks undermining efforts to educate and train the next generation of providers, practitioners and professionals that our economy depends on,” a university spokesperson said in a statement. 
 Stephani Clark, a second-year clinical psychology doctoral student at Alliant University, opted to live with her mother to save costs, though rising gas prices have increased her travel expenses.
 Clark is paying for her program, which costs roughly $23,000 a year, through the expiring Grad PLUS program. Without that program, Clark wouldn’t have been able to obtain that degree, and she worries what that will mean for her future students.
 “Black women hold a very small percentage of the field of clinical psychology. I would love to see more people that look like me in this position, but with the concerns of affordability, there are barriers that will deter people from pursuing this pathway,” Clark said.
 Private lenders will see more business
 One group set to benefit from the new loan limits are private lenders. Student loan originations through SoFi nearly doubled, to $2.9 billion, compared to the previous year, the private lender reported last month. 
 Private lenders, who expect to see more business from borrowers after the rules went into effect earlier this year, welcomed the changes, said Norman Rodriguez, the director of school lending with the private loan refinancing company Ignyte by Yrefy. 
 “This pressure from the current administration is going to be really painful for families in the short term,” Rodriguez said. “But in the long term, I think it’s going to leave us with a society that is more conscious in our decisions in education.” 
 For medical and law school, federal loans are limited to $50,000 each year and $200,000 in total. Graduate programs have even lower limits. Students attending medical school in California, where programs can cost well over $100,000 per year, may have to turn to private lenders to fill the gap, or forgo pursuing that career.
 Ryan Coryea, who recently graduated from UC San Diego with a political science degree, had hoped to attend graduate or law school to advance her career and secure a higher-paying job. 
 Coryea is concerned that she would have to turn to private lenders, which come with higher interest rates and have fewer protections than federal loans, to cover the total cost of graduate school. She is reluctant to take that risk at a time when the cost of living remains high.
 “I’m probably just gonna move home and keep saving,” she said. “And without going back to school, I’ll probably just have to do that for at least a few years, which sounds sad to say, but it’s really just the truth.”
